title: When A Startup Sells, Its Employees’ Equity Plans Can Change Overnight
summary: By Ron Honig Acquisitions are reshaping the technology industry. Venture-backed AI companies acquired 195 AI startups this year through late September , already exceeding the total for all of 2025, Crunchbase data shows. For investors and founders, such acquisitions can represent major financial milestones. For employees holding equity compensation, a transaction can also change personal financial plans they had expected to follow for years. A client whose employer was acquired in an all-cash transaction described to me the atmosphere inside the company during the weeks that followed: Employees repeatedly discussed the deal in office corridors, trying to understand what it meant for their equity awards, their jobs and their future. She compared the confusion to the atmosphere surrounding a major reorganization or a round of layoffs. The transaction offered the prospect of substantial financial gains. Yet employees were struggling to establish what those gains would mean for them individually. One acquisition, different outcomes Ron Honig, co-CEO of From-Honig Family Office.

payload.text: By Ron Honig Acquisitions are reshaping the technology industry. Venture-backed AI companies acquired 195 AI startups this year through late September , already exceeding the total for all of 2025, Crunchbase data shows. For investors and founders, such acquisitions can represent major financial milestones. For employees holding equity compensation, a transaction can also change personal financial plans they had expected to follow for years. A client whose employer was acquired in an all-cash transaction described to me the atmosphere inside the company during the weeks that followed: Employees repeatedly discussed the deal in office corridors, trying to understand what it meant for their equity awards, their jobs and their future. She compared the confusion to the atmosphere surrounding a major reorganization or a round of layoffs. The transaction offered the prospect of substantial financial gains. Yet employees were struggling to establish what those gains would mean for them individually. One acquisition, different outcomes Ron Honig, co-CEO of From-Honig Family Office. Employees at the same company can emerge from an acquisition with remarkably different financial outcomes. Some own vested shares. Others hold restricted stock units, stock options or performance-based awards. Their rights depend on grant agreements, vesting conditions and transaction terms. Even two employees holding RSUs may face different payment schedules or employment requirements. Depending on the agreements, outstanding awards may be settled in cash, accelerated, converted into replacement awards, or remain subject to future conditions. One employee might receive a substantial payment when the transaction closes. Another may have much of the expected value tied to continued employment. The announced acquisition price provides a reference point. It rarely tells an individual employee everything they need to know about the money they will receive. This helps explain the conversations my client described. Colleagues may compare the value of their equity without realizing that their contractual rights differ. Wealth and employment uncertainty Technology employees with substantial equity compensation often depend on their employer in several ways. Their salaries, bonuses, career opportunities and investment portfolios may all be linked to the same company. An all-cash acquisition can reduce their exposure to its share price once vested shares are converted into cash. Other forms of dependence may continue. The acquiring company may reorganize teams, change responsibilities or introduce retention arrangements. Employees whose unvested awards remain conditional on employment may face difficult choices about staying. Someone expecting a large payment can therefore feel financially stronger while becoming less certain about their career. Before making plans A major acquisition announcement can change personal ambitions long before the proceeds arrive. Employees may begin considering early retirement, a new business, a career break or a major family purchase. Those possibilities are worth exploring. But an announced acquisition may still require regulatory approvals and other closing conditions. The headline value of an equity award may differ substantially from the cash ultimately available to its holder. Taxes, exercise costs where applicable, outstanding liabilities and payment schedules can all affect the outcome. So can the employee’s financial position outside the company. A substantial payment might make a career change affordable without providing enough capital to fund permanent retirement. Existing pension savings, household spending and future earning capacity remain important. In my work with technology executives, I have seen expectations about new wealth reshape personal plans before the underlying numbers have been established. Employees facing a cash acquisition can begin with three questions: What rights do my specific awards provide? When will the proceeds actually become available? And what choices will the resulting after-tax capital support? The answers may differ considerably among colleagues. An exit without an exit decision Founders who sell their companies often participate directly in negotiating the transaction. Employees holding equity compensation generally have much less influence over its timing. They may have intended to retain their shares for years, sell gradually or remain employed until additional awards vested. A corporate acquisition can replace those plans with a timetable established by the transaction. For some employees, the result will be substantial financial flexibility. For others, a significant part of their expected compensation may remain connected to future employment. The period between announcement and closing can be especially difficult because the financial opportunity is visible while important details remain unresolved. My client’s description of the office corridors captured that experience. The company had made a decision about its future. Its employees were left to work out what that decision meant for theirs. The acquisition determines the terms of a corporate transaction. Each employee still has to establish how much financial freedom it creates. Ron Honig is co-CEO and managing partner of From-Honig Family Office , which works with technology executives, founders and families on integrated wealth planning, equity compensation and major liquidity events. His background includes more than two decades in the technology industry. Disclosure: The views expressed are the author’s own. This article is for general informational purposes and does not constitute financial, investment, legal or tax advice. Details of the client experience have been presented without identifying information. payload.text: Before James Kim evaluated education startups, he used their products in his classroom. The Reach Capital partner began his career as a high school math teacher with Teach For America after studying astrophysics at Yale . He later worked in college access and Yale admissions, and earned graduate degrees in business and education from Stanford before joining Reach. As a teacher, he was an early user of ClassDojo , an experience he describes as “game-changing.” James Kim, partner at Reach Capital. (Courtesy photo) His investment firm, Reach Capital, has also evolved. Founded in 2015 after spinning out of NewSchools Venture Fund , the San Francisco-based firm initially focused on technology for K-12 schools and districts. Its mandate has since expanded to learning, health and work, with investments in companies including ClassDojo, Cartwheel , Stepful and Replit . In August, Reach announced its fifth fund, a $265 million vehicle that brought its assets under management to nearly $1 billion. The firm, which has backed more than 180 companies, plans to invest in approximately 50 additional teams through the new fund, targeting pre-seed, seed and Series A rounds. Crunchbase News spoke with Kim about how Reach’s education roots inform its broader strategy, what it saw in AI detection company GPTZero , and why some of its best investments initially divided its own team. We also discussed how ownership stakes and secondary transactions have shaped the firm’s approach to returning capital. This interview has been edited for length and clarity. Crunchbase News: You started your career as a high school math teacher. How did that shape your view of education technology? Kim: I taught ninth through 12th grade, mostly Algebra I and geometry. I was very early to ClassDojo. Back then, it was a very simple classroom management tool, and it was game-changing for me. It has since evolved into a sprawling suite, but I already knew technology could move the needle. Reach began as an education investor. How did the firm’s focus evolve into learning, health and work? Kim: Reach started in 2015, and our original focus was exclusively on learning and education technology — more specifically, technology sold into schools and districts. Our founding partners were seeing the growth of devices in schools, one-to-one device ratios and broadband penetration. The belief was that you would start to see a proliferation of technology serving students, teachers and administrators and moving the needle on learning outcomes. That is what ended up playing out. Some of our early bets are now household names in edtech, such as Newsela , Nearpod and ClassDojo. Reach spun out of NewSchools Venture Fund, where three of our four founding partners had started doing for-profit seed investing before 2015. Over time, we branched out from K-12 into higher education, and then into consumer learning. We also started getting pulled toward healthcare and work. Health and wellbeing affect a learner’s readiness for the classroom, so we were being pulled toward mental health, behavioral health and developmental health. On the work side, formal learning typically ends in college, but you still need the bridge to a job. Once you’re on the job, you need to continue learning, especially in the current environment. A few years ago, we officially put a stake in the ground and said we invest across learning, health and work. The common thread is that these are the most important systems underlying human development and flourishing. So far, the breakdown has been roughly 50% learning, 25% health and 25% work. These sectors have different buyers, regulations and business models. What did investing in education teach you that translates to healthcare and work? Kim: Education is highly regulated, and institutional buying is complex. Many stakeholders must provide input, and decisions often require board-level approval. We were familiar with and comfortable with regulated products and complex go-to-market motions. Selling to a university or a K-12 district, in terms of the complexity and the need to intersect with regulation and policy, is quite comparable to selling to a health system, hospital or insurance carrier. Cartwheel is a good example of where our experience gave us an advantage. It provides mental health teletherapy, but the customer is the school district and the care setting is in schools. While we were relatively new to behavioral health when we made that investment, we were very familiar with selling to school districts and implementing an intervention within a school setting. That gave us an advantage both in winning the investment opportunity and supporting the company afterward. Reach talks about “elevating human potential.” What makes an investment fit that mandate? Kim: We look for products and services that increase access to quality education, quality care or quality earnings, or some combination of those. We really have to see the mechanism for that happening. It’s not good enough to be pitched a SaaS or AI product and have the founders say, “This will make people more productive at work, and therefore maybe they will earn more or enjoy their jobs more.” That’s plausible, but it isn’t a good enough theory of how the product actually increases access to quality earnings. Several teammates, including myself, are former educators. We care about meaningful, needle-moving impact. We address access from both the demand side and the supply side. On the demand side, we build products that create delightful, impactful experiences for consumers: Brilliant , Stepful’s allied healthcare training, and Replit for what its founder calls “citizen developers.” On the supply side, it’s helping schools, health systems and companies function more efficiently and effectively. WorkWhile , for example, helps logistics and hospitality companies hire hourly workers better and treat them better. We think about the problem from both sides of the market. Reach backed GPTZero, which agreed to join Superhuman . Was that an investment in solving a problem created by AI? Kim: That wasn’t actually our investment thesis. In my opinion, they have the best AI detector on the market. But their thesis was that AI use in education should not be banned. It shouldn’t be punitive or become a cat-and-mouse game between the educator and the learner. Since all of us as professionals use AI in our jobs, students should learn how to use it responsibly and thoughtfully. It was the first AI detector company I had seen with that positioning, as opposed to helping schools, districts and universities clamp down on AI usage. That’s why I liked it. I don’t see it as a problem for students to use AI for certain purposes, such as brainstorming, organizing thoughts and editing. GPTZero helps educators work with students and teach them how to use AI responsibly. Do you see other opportunities to build companies around the problems AI creates? Kim: Yes, most notably in AI governance and evaluations. Going back to regulated categories, you need to make sure AI is not irresponsibly using personally identifiable information in education or healthcare. Those categories have very strict regulations, and infrastructure companies are emerging to help ensure AI products interact with that data responsibly. I do think there are opportunities for large, successful, profitable companies to be created in response to the problems AI creates. What does GPTZero’s sale tell you about which AI products can become durable standalone companies and which belong within larger platforms? Kim: I don’t know whether GPTZero is an example of either. They had been fielding acquisition offers from pretty early on. This particular opportunity arose earlier this year, and there was a compelling synergy story with Superhuman, formerly Grammarly . The founders and the board agreed that it made sense to combine the companies. But they could just as easily have remained standalone. There is another AI detection company called Pangram that’s quite good and is still a standalone, venture-backed company. It’s not clear to me that this category can’t exist on its own. We have to be very case-by-case. We don’t know until we see the trajectory, financial sustainability and evolution of the market, whether it makes sense to explore a strategic acquisition or grow independently and perhaps one day become a publicly traded company. Reach has backed more than 180 companies. What patterns have you noticed among those that exceeded expectations? Kim: The reality of venture is that a very small share of investments yields the overwhelming majority of returns. Given the outlier nature of those successes, it’s hard to identify unifying principles that always predict a successful exit. If we could, we would only make those investments. But there are a few things we think are somewhat common across our wins. One is a very smart, gritty, genuinely mission-driven founder or founding team, often with a strong personal connection to the problem. Second is some sort of nonconsensus insight about the market. That often comes from experiencing the problem themselves, sometimes as practitioners in the industry — a former educator, for example. Third is a defensible and scalable business model. The nonconsensus insight is funny because it’s what makes these companies look weird and maybe uninvestable in the beginning. Even within our team, they’re often the most polarizing opportunities. You look at the votes, and a bunch of people vote no, but it gets just enough yeses to pass. Then, 10 years later, it’s one of our best investments. People lose sight of this in the current environment, but the best opportunities are often the most nonconsensus. Those can be the most creative and interesting founders, and you can get in at reasonable valuations early and help them become consensus bets. Reach says its first two funds have returned investors’ capital. What produced those returns? Kim: We’re no exception to the power-law distribution in venture. Our first fund has been returned 2.2x by literally two investments. Our second fund has been returned 1.2x by one investment. These are cash distributions, by the way. Especially in the second fund, there’s still remaining value, so we’ll see how high that number gets. One fund-returning exit would be great; two or three would be amazing. That’s what we’re striving for. How has that experience changed your approach to ownership and follow-on investing? Kim: We’ve had some great exits where, given how prominent the company is, you might be surprised that our share of the returns wasn’t that large. That’s purely an ownership calculation. From our first fund to today, we’ve meaningfully increased our initial ownership target. We now try to get as close to 15% ownership upfront as possible. That means writing slightly bigger checks and reserving relatively less for follow-on investments and more for the initial check. It’s important for the exit math and distribution math. What role do secondary transactions play in getting liquidity? We’ve become very proactive and conscientious about liquidity opportunities. Much of our distributions to investors come from secondary sales — selling our shares in a subsequent round, before an actual exit. Whenever there’s an opportunity, we evaluate it. We consider how long we’ve been in the company, how much we can get out, and how much upside we think remains. As companies stay private longer, early-stage investors are achieving liquidity much more often through secondary transactions. I like to think we were early to that trend, but it’s certainly mainstream now. Sometimes, when we see enough upside, we’ll buy secondary shares. GPTZero was an example: After our Series A investment, we bought secondary shares, and I’m really glad we did because it worked out well. For us, we sell more often, but occasionally we buy. payload.text: By Nacho De Marco Today’s venture capital ecosystem looks markedly different from even just five years ago. Most significantly, a small number of AI companies are now attracting the vast majority of available venture capital. In Q1 2026, just four companies collectively raised $188 billion , which alone accounted for 65% of total global venture investment, per Crunchbase data. Meanwhile, in that same quarter, just 20% of global VC funding went to non-AI firms . Deal count was also down 30%, meaning that checks are being made out to fewer companies all around. So what happens to startups when the VC route is all but closed? I built a company into a multibillion-dollar business without any venture funding. Here’s a few lessons I picked up along the way: Prioritize customers and revenue, not fundraising Nacho De Marco, founding GP of BDev Ventures, and chairman of BairesDev. Many founders unknowingly treat fundraising as a measure of success. But while it’s useful, funding doesn’t result in success on its own. Achieving strong levels of customer trust is also helpful when it comes to inspiring investor confidence. High retention rates, repeat purchases and sustained engagement drive the  financial fundamentals on which strong valuations are built. In B2B SaaS, for instance, companies with net revenue retention above 110% are valued at 2.4x the median . Additionally, customers provide a feedback loop that helps create the discipline every company needs, and each user is a vote of confidence that compounds over time. Going to market: Take time on pricing strategy Too many early-stage companies set prices too low because they fear that higher prices will repel customers. In my experience, however, underpricing more often signals uncertainty rather than good value. Customers want quality products and services, and they expect that the quality will be reflected in the price. Incredibly, only 22% of B2B SaaS firms conduct rigorous pricing research , and firms more commonly regret underpricing than overpricing. So at the outset, it’s important for startups to inform themselves what price their product or service can actually sustain, and then raise quality if it’s too low. Equally, in services markets where prices are more established around a norm, superior quality can be an important differentiator. At the same time, however, companies must continually resist the temptation to chase customers with ever-cheaper prices, which can start a race to the bottom. Hire the best talent Too many founders hire for speed rather than quality. Take the time needed to raise the bar with talent. Hire the right people, and they’ll help maximize every last drop of value. Many years ago, I decided to focus on just a small fraction of our applicants and hire only the top 1% of talent . When we found the best developers, it meant we could compete on delivery quality rather than just price. Keeping costs low is important, but skimping on talent is not a winning strategy. Use process automation efficiencies to drive growth One of our best decisions was to replace manual hiring processes with proprietary machine-learning systems at an early stage. Not only do these systems screen developer applications, but they can also build, match and deploy top-quality teams for each client project. This advance allowed us to cut costs associated with evaluating applications, accelerate lead times, and improve the quality of our teamwork. In parallel, we also invested in creating similar systems for our digital marketing so that growth wouldn’t require proportional increases in overhead. Whether it’s in recruitment, sales or operations, process automation can create some of the biggest drivers of growth and help bring about conditions needed for significant expansion to occur. Operate as if cash is running out tomorrow Companies thrive in challenging funding environments by operating with discipline. That means obsessing over unit economics, prioritizing activities that directly drive revenue, questioning every cost, and eliminating anything that isn’t pulling its weight. Not only does this aid growth, but it also makes a business more resilient in hard times. Financial constraints drive leaders to create efficiencies by automating workflows, streamlining processes and inventing innovative work models. Years before COVID-19 forced others to follow our lead, our company streamlined its operations and boosted scalability by developing a remote-working model. When the pandemic made remote work necessary, the fact that we already had the systems and workflows in place gave us a competitive advantage over other firms, and this in turn led to significant growth. Long term: Stay married to the problem, not the solution The past decade convinced many founders that venture capital was the default path to building a meaningful company. But while funding cycles rise and fall, the fundamental principles of good business don’t. Infusions of capital can accelerate growth, but they cannot create a great company from scratch. On the longest timescale, the most successful founders are the ones committed to solving problems rather than just selling a product and chasing funding. In a world short on funding, growth simply can’t happen without it. Nacho De Marco is the founding GP of BDev Ventures , and chairman of BairesDev , one of the largest bootstrapped nearshoring companies worldwide. Driven by his entrepreneurial spirit, he launched BDev Ventures in 2021 to help B2B companies accelerate their growth through a proprietary lead-generation platform. He also invests in and serves on the boards of biotechnology and e-learning companies. In recognition of his career path, he won distinctions such as an EY Entrepreneur Of The Year 2024 Bay Area Award. payload.text: Venture funding into fintech startups slid 21.4% year over year in the third quarter of 2026, while deal count fell nearly 31%, Crunchbase data shows, pointing to a narrower funding market with fewer rounds and continued reliance on large transactions. All told, fintech startups raised $10.6 billion globally in the third quarter of 2026, down 28.4% from $14.9 billion in Q2 2026 and 21.4% from $13.5 billion in Q3 2025. The pullback comes as investors draw sharper distinctions between companies attracting capital and those struggling to raise, according to QED Investors partner Laura Bock . “The market remains bifurcated — AI vs. not and market leaders vs. not,” she said. Forerunner founder Kirsten Green similarly described capital concentrating in fewer, larger rounds, with infrastructure, payments and stablecoin rails attracting investor interest, supported by greater regulatory clarity. Deal count drops Notably, deal count in Q3 was the lowest in the quarters covered by our analysis, dating back to the first quarter of 2018. Just 687 fintech funding rounds were recorded globally in the third quarter, compared with 789 in the previous quarter and 995 in the same period a year earlier. That represents declines of 12.9% quarter over quarter and 31% year over year. Investors are demanding stronger evidence of performance before writing checks, noted Green. For Series A and B rounds, “evidence counts for more than narrative,” she said. In emerging categories, actual usage and momentum can matter more than revenue multiples. Elsewhere, investors want efficient growth, a credible path to profitability and stronger evidence of lasting customer demand before committing to a large Series B, Green said. More startups are also combining debt and equity to limit dilution. Pullback in large rounds The quarter-over-quarter funding decline was largely driven by a pullback in large rounds. Funding from rounds of at least $100 million fell 43.3%, from $9.07 billion in Q2 to $5.15 billion in Q3, accounting for approximately 93% of the overall dollar decline. Funding from rounds below $100 million declined just 5.1% sequentially. Compared with Q3 2025, funding from rounds of at least $100 million decreased 7%, while funding from smaller rounds fell 31.4%. Large transactions remained more resilient than smaller-round funding year over year. That divide also extends to pricing. Green said a small group of companies with clear momentum command aggressive valuations, while others face greater discipline. Bock pointed to Ramp and Monzo as similarly sized businesses with widely different valuations, attributing Ramp’s premium to investor enthusiasm for its AI momentum and growth trajectory. Global mega-rounds The United States remained the largest market for fintech funding last quarter. All told, U.S. startups attracted $5.38 billion, or 50.5% of the $10.64 billion global total in Q3. The next-largest markets were Singapore with $1.28 billion (12.1%); Saudi Arabia with $626.6 million (5.9%); India with $452 million (4.2%); Brazil with $352 million (3.3%); and the United Kingdom with $337.8 million (3.2%). Singapore’s total was heavily concentrated in Ant International ’s $1.2 billion round. Despite the U.S. being the largest market for fintech funding, the quarter’s five largest funding rounds went to companies based outside the United States, ironically. Ant International, a Singapore-based provider of digital payments and financial services for businesses, raised the largest round in Q3 2026, a $1.2 billion Series A at a listed $11.2 billion post-money valuation. The data does not identify a lead investor but lists Alibaba Group and Ant Group as participants. Barq , a financial app provider based in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, raised a $329.5 million Series A at a $1.85 billion post-money valuation. M20 Capital , Noon Investments and Sohar International participated in the financing. Hong Kong-based Qupital , which provides financing to e-commerce businesses, secured a $300 million Series C led by M Capital at an estimated $1.36 billion post-money valuation. Jakarta, Indonesia-based Ajaib , an online investing platform, raised a $270 million Series C led by SBI Group at a $1.35 billion post-money valuation. Rounding out the top five, Riyadh-based Tabby , a digital financial services provider, raised $233 million in a Series F round led by Blue Pool Capital at a $6.5 billion post-money valuation. Late-stage fintech funding fell to $4.8 billion, down 40.4% quarter over quarter and 17.3% year over year, in Q3, per Crunchbase data. One startup lifts early-stage funding Early-stage fintech funding was comparatively resilient at $4.23 billion, up 11% quarter over quarter and down just 0.6% year over year. However, Ant International’s $1.2 billion Series A accounted for 28.4% of that total. Excluding that transaction from Q3 2026 alone, early-stage funding would have fallen 20.4% sequentially and 28.8% year over year. Early-stage deal count also dropped, from 173 in Q2 to 165 in Q3, suggesting that the increase in funding dollars did not reflect a broad expansion in activity. Fundraising expectations are rising as AI makes products faster to build and launch, Bock said. Early revenue carries less weight than sustained growth. While $1 million in annual recurring revenue once served as a common Series A benchmark, investors now want greater traction and stronger momentum, including revenue that has at least tripled over six months. “Efficiency still matters, but growth is back in focus,” she said, adding that expectations of larger potential outcomes are pushing valuations higher. Meanwhile, angel and seed funding totaled $1.12 billion, down 19.7% from Q2 and 35.2% from Q3 2025. AI reshapes investor priorities AI is primarily redirecting investment within fintech, although agents and payments are attracting some new capital, Green said. Companies without an obvious AI offering can still raise funding, but investors increasingly expect evidence that the technology improves their economics, speed or ability to reach customers. “The product has to carry that story,” she said. Bock said the distinction between companies adding AI to existing processes and those building their products around it matters. The strongest AI products deliver substantial improvements that drive rapid adoption and customers’ willingness to pay. “When investors say a company is ‘AI,’ they usually mean its growth rate is high, so growth has become the proxy,” she said. QED’s recent investments span customer support, analytics, financial advice, banking infrastructure and fraud prevention. Bock sees a durable opportunity for startups that handle the specialized integrations and accuracy requirements financial services demands — work she argues frontier AI labs are unlikely to prioritize. Green, meanwhile, said payments initiated by AI agents have moved “from ‘if’ to ‘when’” in her conversations, as major networks and processors introduced protocols to support them. She is also seeing more fintech companies seek ownership of regulated infrastructure rather than rely on outside providers. But she sees potential overfunding in stablecoin infrastructure, where many startups are pursuing the same customers, and in tools that let AI agents complete purchases for buyers, where, in her view, startup formation has outpaced transaction volume. Green sees more opportunity in the systems that make agent-driven commerce trustworthy, including fraud prevention, identity verification, agent permissions and tools that help merchants accept those purchases. “I suspect the market is treating the rails as the moat,” she said. In her view, payment infrastructure is likely to become commoditized, leaving more value with the companies that own customer relationships and earn their trust. Bock’s broader thesis is that AI could reshape financial services by sharply reducing the costs of underwriting, compliance and customer service while enabling more personalized financial products. QED is particularly interested in advice and wealth management, underwriting, insurance claims, risk and compliance, and finance back-office operations, alongside stablecoins and tokenization. “The financial services operating system will be rebuilt end-to-end,” she said. payload.text: A continued boom in late-stage and growth funding combined with a surge in seed-stage funding helped buoy venture investment in Latin America for the third quarter of 2026, Crunchbase data shows. All told, startups in Latin America raised a combined $1.3 billion across seed- and growth-stage deals in the three-month period ending Sept. 30. That was up 26% year over year but down 9% from the second quarter. For perspective, we charted out total investment, color-coded by stage, for the past 12 quarters below. Of the quarterly total, $757 million went into late-stage and growth deals, up 74% compared to the $435 million that flowed into such deals in the third quarter of 2025. However, that is down 21.3% from the $962 million in late-stage and growth rounds raised by LatAm startups in the second quarter. (Although it’s worth noting that Q2 2026 represented the most raised at that stage since the second quarter of 2022.) Mexico startups have raised $1.52 billion in venture funding during the first three quarters of 2026, per Crunchbase data. Notably, that’s about 40.7% more than the $1.08 billion Brazil’s startups raised in the same period. This is unusual as Brazil has historically been the largest recipient of venture funding in Latin America. Still, Brazil continues to attract a broad range of investors. “Over the past year, we have seen investments into Brazil from firms including Sequoia , Founders Fund , NEA , Battery and Tidemark ,” Allen Taylor , managing partner of Endeavor Catalyst , told Crunchbase News. “For several, this marked either their first investment in Latin America or their first in a long time.” Igor Piquet , Endeavor Catalyst’s vice president and head of Latin America, noted that Mexico drew more venture funding in the first half of 2026 than Brazil. But much of Mexico’s funding went to a few startups, he pointed out, while Brazil recorded many deals. “Investors are concentrating on a few Mexican winners, while Brazil retains the breadth,” Piquet said, adding that Brazil also leads in realized exits. Table of contents Outsized rounds An uptick in seed funding ‘Another rediscovery moment’ Methodology Glossary of funding terms Outsized rounds Several mega-raises took place in Latin America in the third quarter. And notably, the two largest funding deals were not for companies in Brazil or Mexico, which have historically raised the largest share of venture capital in the region. They also weren’t to fintech, which typically has the most funding recipients in the region, but rather to energy-related startups. Black Giant , the Chilean project company for EnergyX ’s Black Giant lithium project, raised $225 million in a July round at a reported $900 million valuation. And Colombia’s Erco Energía , a clean energy company that builds and operates solar power systems for homes and businesses, landed a $129 million Series C in August at a reported $600 million valuation. Mexico’s Kapital , an AI-powered financial services company, raised a $125 million Series C in September at a $1.6 billion valuation. Tru Arrow Partners led the financing, which included a senior debt funding facility provided by Fasanara Capital . And in August, Brazilian fintech Kesh Bank brought in $106.9 million in an equity and debt seed round at a $626 million valuation. Also in August, Brazil’s Decade , an AI-native wealth advisory company, landed $85 million in  what Crunchbase data shows is the largest seed funding deal ever raised for a Latin American startup. Founded by Vitor Olivier , former CTO of Nubank , and Felipe Meneses , founder of Hyperplane AI , the startup is backed by Benchmark , Greenoaks , Diffusion , Norte Ventures and Atlantico . An uptick in seed funding Latin America experienced a marked surge in very early-stage funding totals in the third quarter, largely thanks to the seed rounds mentioned above. Of the $1.3 billion raised by Latin America’s startups in the third quarter, about 20.5% — or $266 million — was raised across the angel and seed stages. That’s up 128% from the $117 million raised across those stages in the second quarter of 2026, and up 62% from the $165 million in the same quarter last year. Just over 22%, or $288 million, was raised at early stages, down 18.9% from $355 million in the second quarter and 34% from $437 million in the same period last year. We expect the Q3 deal counts to rise somewhat over time; however, as seed rounds in particular are commonly reported weeks or months after they close. ‘Another rediscovery moment’ Latin America is drawing renewed interest from international venture investors, according to Endeavor’s Taylor. He said international VCs were more active in the region, particularly Brazil, during the first three quarters of 2026 than in 2024 and 2025 combined, through both new investments and follow-on funding. “I joke that investors from the U.S. ‘rediscover’ Latin America every five or six years, and I think we are approaching another rediscovery moment,” Taylor told Crunchbase News. Endeavor Catalyst recently closed its oversubscribed $320 million fifth fund. Latin America accounts for nearly 40% of its portfolio by both deals and dollars, and Fund V had made 14 investments in the region as of Sept. 22. Taylor also pointed to opportunities beyond Brazil and Mexico, including repeat founders building global businesses from Colombia and emerging companies in Venezuela and Central America. Liquidity is improving, although acquisitions and secondary transactions are providing more opportunities than public listings, Piquet said. He pointed to approximately 60 private Latin American technology companies that have each raised at least $150 million as a potential pipeline for future IPOs. “The exit door is open, although it is not primarily opening through IPOs yet,” Piquet said. Taylor expects more exits could help bring global investors back consistently, with potential New York Stock Exchange listings by companies such as Wellhub , CloudWalk or Creditas contributing to another “rediscovery moment” in 2027. International investors remain interested in Latin America but have become more selective about deploying capital, according to Ana Cristina Gadala-Maria of QED Investors . Firms with a longstanding presence in the region remain engaged, while many that entered during the 2020–2021 investment boom have shifted toward AI opportunities elsewhere and are concentrating on existing portfolios, she noted. “Global investors are increasingly investing behind themes rather than geographies,” she said, putting Latin American startups in more direct competition with companies in the U.S. and other markets. Investor interest is increasingly centered on AI-native businesses and financial infrastructure, particularly stablecoins and cross-border payments. Gadala-Maria said more founders are targeting global markets from the outset, marking a departure from the previous wave of startups that adapted established business models to underserved local markets. “Increasingly, we’re seeing founders build globally competitive technology companies from Latin America, rather than necessarily for Latin America,” she said. Gadala-Maria agrees that Brazil and Mexico remain the region’s largest markets, with Brazil offering a deeper, more mature startup ecosystem and Mexico providing substantial room for financial services innovation. She pointed to Argentina as an overlooked market, citing its strong technical talent and founders building companies for global customers. payload.text: By Anurag Gurtu Congratulations to the enterprise AI company that just raised another nine-figure round to solve a problem software is supposed to solve by itself: getting humans to use the product. You know the one. Won’t name it. Don’t have to. You’ve read the press release — “autonomous,” “agentic,” “category-defining” in paragraph one, and then, a few paragraphs down, where the money is actually going: hiring an army of engineers to sit inside customer offices and manually make the “autonomous” thing behave. Nothing says “we’ve built the future of work” quite like raising half a billion dollars to hire more people to do the work. The business model, decoded Anurag Gurtu, co-founder and CEO of Airrived. Here’s how it works, in case the deck was too artfully vague: Sell the customer an “AI platform.” Discover the platform doesn’t actually do the thing on its own. Send in the forward deployed engineers: sharp young people with CS degrees who now spend six months hand-building the workflow the website implied already existed. Bill the customer for “software.” Book it as ARR. Raise a bigger round because “ARR go up.” Repeat, forever, with an increasingly large and increasingly expensive engineering org standing between the product and the promise it made. This is not a flywheel. This is a payroll with a pitch deck. And the industry has stopped even pretending otherwise — it’s fundraising on it, loudly. OpenAI pledged up to $1.5 billion into a deployment joint venture valued at $10 billion, with another $4 billion from TPG , Bain Capital , Advent , Brookfield and Goanna . The vehicle, DeployCo, has been reported with more than $4 billion in investment. Meanwhile, job postings for “forward deployed engineer” are up somewhere between 800% and 1,000% year over year. Lightcast data reported by Fortune put the increase at more than 1,000% from January to August 2026. Financial Times data carried by PYMNTS put listings up more than 800% from January to September 2025, and Indeed data showed postings rising from 643 in April 2025 to 5,330 in April 2026. Total comp is pushing past $300,000 in the U.S. Employer postings list Anthropic at $280,000 to $320,000 base pay and OpenAI at $185,000 to $300,000 base, plus equity. Fortune reported some Anthropic roles reaching $400,000 in total compensation. Somewhere, a VC is calling this “operating leverage” with a completely straight face. It is not operating leverage. It’s a staffing agency that learned to say “agentic.” The tell Ask the one question the pitch deck conveniently never answers: “If you pulled the embedded engineer out tomorrow, does the customer still get what they paid for?” If the honest answer is “well, no, but the ARR is real” — that’s not product-market fit. That’s people-market fit, and people-market fit has a brutally unglamorous ceiling: You can only hire humans so fast, and you can never hire them cheap enough to earn a software multiple. Every new logo doesn’t get more profitable to serve. It gets another headcount request. Two companies, same $20 million ARR. One needs 10 engineers to keep the lights on. The other needs 100. Both slides say, “AI software company.” The difference shows up in gross margin, cost to onboard the next customer, and whether that cost falls as the company scales. The bill always comes due Here’s the thing about people-market fit: it feels great right up until someone asks the unfashionable questions: What does it actually cost, fully loaded, to onboard the next customer? Does that number go down as the company scales, or does it just grow the org chart? What happens to gross margin if the first year growth slows and the headcount can’t hide behind hypergrowth anymore? Companies funding their FDE armies with fresh nine-figure rounds are betting nobody asks these questions until after the round closes and the confetti is swept up. That’s a fine bet in a hype cycle. It’s a terrible one in a market that’s about to start reading the fine print. Because eventually, someone always reads the fine print. A CFO builds a cost-per-deployment model. A CIO benchmarks time-to-value against three vendors instead of trusting one demo. An investor finally does the unglamorous work of separating software ARR from human-powered ARR on the same balance sheet. The distinction buyers and investors can test is on the numbers. Software ARR should get cheaper to deliver as it scales. Human-powered ARR does not. OpenAI guaranteed the private-equity backers of its deployment vehicle an annual 17.5% return over five years, which is a different structure from a growth thesis.¹ So no, your AI isn’t autonomous. But your business model might be — autonomously transferring the cost of a services company onto a software valuation, for as long as the music plays. Enjoy the round. Hope the org chart was worth it. Anurag Gurtu , the co-founder and CEO of Airrived , is an entrepreneur and product leader with more than 20 years of experience across cybersecurity and AI. He has built three generative AI companies, including one that reached unicorn status. Gurtu is known for turning advanced AI into scalable, real-world platforms, and previously contributed to successful exits, including acquisitions by Splunk , Tripwire and Sun Microsystems , and a public company, FireEye . He holds a master’s degree from the University of Southern California and CISSP certification. Illustration: Dom Guzman

payload.text: By Eric Francia How would you handle a junior employee questioning the way you’ve always done something? Might you roll your eyes and dismiss their comments as naivety? Or would you indulge their curiosity? As AI has made knowledge accessible on a scale never seen before, companies are becoming leaner and operating faster. What once took a large team months to do can now be done by a handful of people in a few days. It is undeniable that autonomous systems are changing the way we work. In the small and dynamic teams of the future, choosing the right humans to direct your AI systems will become make or break for a company. As a six-time founder, I’ve learned the best workplaces are the ones where questioning things is the norm. Here’s how to build a team that questions orders as much as it obeys them. AI by design Eric Francia, co-founder and CEO of Uniplay. “AI by design” doesn’t only mean building the right autonomous systems. It’s also about creating autonomous humans. You need to trust the human in the loop as much as you do the technology. The team around you ultimately shapes the company in ways you can’t control. So surrounding yourself with people you trust to make decisions when you’re not in the room is critical to success. The nature of job roles is changing. A job description can be totally different from the one advertised by the time you’ve found a candidate, and a six-month roadmap is outdated by the time you’ve finished drawing it up. The World Economic Forum has stated that 59% of employees will need to reskill by 2030 as AI reshapes the workplace. Hiring for a fixed set of skills won’t move the needle. The people worth investing in are those who are able to learn what comes next. Hire for curiosity Curiosity is the best trait you can hire for. When I look at a CV, it’s not just experience or academic credentials that draw me in. I look for what people have built on the side. What have they made on their own initiative? Hire for curiosity, and you’ll create an environment where people are willing to throw new ideas around and challenge outdated ways of doing things. If your team is worried about saying the wrong thing, they won’t end up saying the right thing either. In a world where technology is turning everything on its head, the companies that will thrive are the ones with curious people who are able to adapt to change quickly. Hand over real responsibility Employees with autonomy operate faster. They make better decisions because company vision is not abstract to people who are given real responsibility to drive it. Being involved in strategic direction stitches an employee into the fabric of the company and keeps them engaged. Trust your employees to know what isn’t working. Allow people to pursue new ideas and reinvent things. Your employees are likely to spot potential problems before you do when they’re closer to the product. Make sure your team has the autonomy to try to fix them before they take hold. Boredom is a big business risk As companies become smaller, employee retention is more important than ever. Losing your best people is costlier when you have fewer of them to begin with. The effects of a bored employee surface quickly in a small team. Boredom makes talented people a little bit slower, and a lot less likely to try the difficult thing. The challenge for modern leaders is keeping your team engaged and interested. A bored employee is more likely to be swayed by a flattering LinkedIn recruiter. Make sure to invest in development, keep your team learning, and always encourage curiosity. Give people autonomy and responsibility from the beginning, and boredom has nowhere to take hold. The mentality of risk and the drive to challenge something outdated is what you need to succeed in the changing work environment. Dare to be a beginner, and teach your team to do the same. That junior employee questioning how you’ve always done things could be the most valuable person in the room. Eric Francia is co-founder and CEO of Stockholm-based Uniplay , an agent-driven, game-based learning platform. He has experience building, exiting and scaling digital companies across 70 countries. Uniplay is his sixth company to date. Illustration: Dom Guzman

title: Omnara
summary: Open-Source Alternative to Claude Managed Agents

extra.author: kmansm27
extra.original_title: Show HN: Omnara – Open-Source Alternative to Claude Managed Agents

story_text.value:
Hey y'all, Kartik from Omnara (https://omnara.com) here. We're building an open-source API for running durable agents. You create an agent with an API call, and Omnara runs the agent loop, gives the agent sandboxes to run commands in, and handles secrets, permissions, and RBAC. Each agent's state is stored in Postgres, so agents survive restarts and cost nothing while idle. You can message them and stream their events over the API.

You may remember us from our early days, when we made a remote-control phone app for Claude Code and Codex. Since the harness ran on a laptop back then, we had to build a relay to reach it, it stopped when the laptop closed, and moving it to a cloud sandbox meant syncing code and agent state between machines. We didn't think remote-controlling a local agent was end-game for how people would run agents, so we built a new product where the agent runs in the cloud, any client can talk to it through an API, and it can still use your laptop as one of its machines.

Anthropic and OpenAI are building hosted versions of this, like Claude Managed Agents and the OpenAI Agents API. Omnara is an open-source version you can run on your own servers and use your own models. It's basically a harness server like the opencode or codex servers, but durable, scalable, with the usual harness features like file and shell tools, subagents, compaction, permission prompts, MCP, skills, memory, yada yada yada.

Here's some interesting architectural decisions we made while building this out:

Most harnesses, like Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, Pi, Goose, etc, run the agent loop in one long-lived process that keeps its log in a JSONL or SQLite file. In Omnara, the log is an append-only event log in Postgres, with inputs, model outputs and tool calls stored as typed rows in their own tables. The loop runs on stateless workers in the control plane. A worker runs one iteration of the loop, either a model call or the tool calls it produced, then releases the agent and puts the next iteration on a queue in Postgres. Whichever worker is free picks it up, so each iteration of an agent's loop can run in a different process on a different machine. Each iteration's result commits in one transaction, so the model output, its tool calls, usage and the next wakeup are saved together or not at all. If a worker dies mid-iteration, nothing commits, its lease expires, and another worker retries it. Agents waiting on a user, a tool or a retry don't hold a worker, so one worker can multiplex thousands of agents.

Also unlike other harnesses, the machines that the workers (our agent loop) run on aren't where the agent runs its commands. Instead, any macOS or Linux machine with an internet connection, like your laptop or any cloud sandbox, can run a small daemon (omnarad) that connects out to Omnara, so it doesn't need any open inbound ports. The agent then gets tools for that machine, like running a command or editing a file. An agent can have any number of machines connected to it. A fun thing I like to do is I have my laptop and a cloud sandbox connected to the same agent, so when my laptop is on, my agent codes there and I can interact with it, and I have it often push to Github. When I close my laptop, my agent sees the laptop went offline, pulls the latest changes to its cloud sandbox, and continues there.

The entire codebase is open source at https://github.com/omnara-ai/omnara, and it’s self hostable, even on a single machine with docker compose. You can also use the hosted version at https://omnara.com. Let me know what you think!

title: buford
summary: I told people I'm a convicted felon after 20 years of hiding it

extra.author: buf
extra.original_title: Show HN: I told people I'm a convicted felon after 20 years of hiding it

story_text.value:
Hi there.

I was engineer number 3 at Eventbrite and founding engineer at Reforge. I've created a dozen or so startups myself and have worked in many others, like Instacart. All this time, no one knew that I was a convicted felon.

It wasn't exactly a topic that came up, but it was certainly something that I never brought up. When you're a convicted felon, people look at you as if you are tainted.

I was unable to rent apartments in San Francisco. I was unable to get a job directly after being released from prison. It's funny because when you owe the state $17,000 in restitution and you can't get a job, people become extremely desperate. And that desperation can easily put you right back into prison.

So I went from homeless person at age 19 to 7-figures about 10 years later. I retired at age 38.

What I'm doing now is writing an autobiography. The main theme of it is hope.

And I want to make sure that people know about it. They don't necessarily have to be interested in it, but if people know about what it's like sleeping in a car believing that one day you will travel the world and then actually doing it, then I think I've accomplished my task in writing this book.

If you're interested, please let me know.

extra.author: themagyar
extra.original_title: Show HN: One click flight booking in Claude

story_text.value:
tldr; Travelers wanted to find and book flights super fast in Claude, so we built this.

--

title: Gauge CLI
summary: Open-Source Hillclimbing for Agent Experience

extra.author: 0x63_Problems
extra.original_title: Show HN: Gauge CLI – Open-Source Hillclimbing for Agent Experience

story_text.value:
Hi HN! We're releasing an open-source CLI for hillclimbing Agent Experience. That means optimizing your agent-facing surfaces (Skills, CLIs, SDKs, and docs) so that your users' coding agents can easily use your product. Pointing your own agent at the repo is enough to get started. https://github.com/gauge-sh/gauge-cli

We've found that power users generally want to hand a CLI/MCP to their agents and get started from the terminal. They rarely want to log in and use the web UI themselves. We think developer tools must be agent-friendly to remain relevant.

Here are some common findings that Gauge identifies:

- agents get confused with CLI/SDK behavior and start source diving - interactive commands block agents - agents use deprecated/old CLI commands - agents don't use Skills when you'd expect - agents confidently assert limitations that don't exist - inconsistent terminology confuses agents - agents can't figure out how commands fit together into a workflow

Locally, the Gauge CLI uses Docker containers to run agent harnesses (you can bring your own subscriptions). It finds where agents get confused or stuck and tests changes using your pre-release artifacts (Skills/CLI etc). We normalize events from Claude Code, Codex, Pi and OpenCode into standardized transcripts, and store them locally, alongside structured information in SQLite so that your agent can easily analyze the data. This enables automatic hillclimbing toward a great Agent Experience.

We also offer hosted compute that enables more features, built on our custom Gateway (for credential brokering and transparent, per-session response rewriting). Hosted compute enables many more concurrent sessions, easier collaboration with teammates, a GitHub App for PR reviews, sessions with logged-in MCPs/APIs, and most importantly it lets you close your laptop while the sessions actually run.

You don't need a Gauge account to run the full loop end-to-end though. We expect that local execution with the CLI is enough to find and fix several agent experience issues in a typical project.

You'll be able to validate fixes for these issues locally, before publishing new versions (we inject pre-release Skills and code artifacts into the sessions).

We would love your feedback!

title: Worklicant
summary: Lightweight ATS. Pay per Vacancy. AI Enabled

extra.author: azyzz228
extra.original_title: Show HN: Worklicant – Lightweight ATS. Pay per Vacancy. AI Enabled

story_text.value:
I have noticed that a lot of job posts that do not use any ATS, and in order to apply, they put their emails and ask candidates to apply with “X” in email subject. That seemed to be very counter productive — imagine having 300+ emails with resumes. Where do you manage them? In Excel? Or how many good candidates you never get to.

I researched popular ATS systems and found out that they require yearly / monthly subscriptions. A lot of them do not have a pricing on the website, so you gotta book a call to be quoted some yearly contract price…

So I built Worklicant — lightweight ATS for tech hiring.

Pay per vacancy. Post a job, share the link, easy application form (no registration needed for applicants). Easy in-app scheduling. Vacancy analytics. Custom hiring stages, tags, notes, application questions.

AI extraction of resume summary, companies, experiences so you do not have to open each resume. You can also write a rejection prompt with ideal candidate description. That will be taken into account when AI (Jev) gives score to each applicant.

I have worked on it for around 2 years on and off so most of the code was hand written (but that’s changing rapidly).

Give it a try and let me know what you think!

title: Jev Cards
summary: Can you beat a vision model at a picture quiz?

extra.author: totisjosema
extra.original_title: Show HN: Jev Cards, Can you beat a vision model at a picture quiz?

story_text.value:
I built a quiz game around TypeSafe's new Jev model, which has vision capabilities. Jev looks at a picture and a question and picks an answer (or taps a place) in about a quarter of a second.

I've always loved quiz games and thought this would be a fun way to see what it can do and how fast it is. I made the cards from scratch, and Jev gets exactly the picture you see. More cards will come over time.

Play against Jev on your own (there's a leaderboard for each mode), or start a live match and challenge your friends, with Jev as one more player.

The code is open source, so feel free to build your own game or make more cards that I can publish.

Play: https://jevcards.com Code: https://github.com/Jose-Sabater/jevcards (the newest cards stay private for a while)

Disclaimer: I ran Jev through both TypeSafe and Opper, and made the cards through Opper's vision models and Claude Code. I work at Opper, but jevcards is open source and free to play.

title: Standard Topic
summary: An AI and RSS-powered news and resource platform

extra.author: johnchoud
extra.original_title: Show HN: Standard Topic – An AI and RSS-powered news and resource platform

story_text.value:
Hi HN,

I'm John, a knowledge management and AI enablement professional. I created Standard Topic, an AI and RSS-powered news and resource platform, with assistance from Claude Code.

Standard Topic uses AI integrations and RSS feeds to curate news and resources across relevant topics and presents these in the form of top stories, trending items, and a curated prompt library to easily gather further context on a given topic (examples of topics being World News, Politics, Business, Technology, Sports, Science, Health and more.)

On topic hubs, you can find a regularly updated at-a-glance AI briefings providing relevant updates, top stories with AI insights and cited sources, and additional recent news coverage. A governance system is in place with AI assisting in ranking stories, retiring items from the top stories section, determining which additional news is displayed, and more.

An AI-generated briefing podcast, in the format of a radio news program, releases each morning and evening (5 AM and 5 PM ET), covering the latest global news.

While in the past I've released apps and websites that felt duct-taped together and which I stopped using after some time, with this one I've actually found myself using it more than Twitter/X and other daily news briefing platforms, while also leading me to more frequently engage directly with publishing platforms cited on Standard Topic.

My recent work in AI has been around finding practical uses in the content and knowledge management areas for integrating the technology, and Standard Topic has developed into what I see as a product that uses structured outputs and automated insights to deliver consistent and trustworthy, cited content while maintaining transparency about being primarily powered by artificial intelligence.

There's still some kinks to work out in terms of automated workflows, design aspects and more.

Let me know what you think!

title: PatchWave
summary: Add static analysis and automerge to Dependabot

extra.author: blimmer
extra.original_title: Show HN: PatchWave - Add static analysis and automerge to Dependabot

story_text.value:
Hey Hacker News, we're Ben, Josh, and Donnie, co-founders of PatchWave.

PatchWave is a GitHub App that combines static analysis and eval'ed agents to analyze and (optionally) auto-merge PRs it deems as safe. If a Dependabot PR breaks your CI build, a fix agent works to get CI passing again.

Dependabot PRs suck. Nobody likes dealing with them. Most of the time they go ignored or a senior engineer spends their valuable time dealing with them. Before PatchWave, I ran a freelance business charging clients hourly to do exactly this kind of "keep the lights on" work. Even at our small startup, we'd spend Monday mornings dealing with Dependabot PRs. Having a human-in-the-loop working with an agent on these PRs was time consuming and, often, agents would get lazy and not actually validate how an upstream change affected the codebase. And, as the quantity and severity of CVEs increases, merging security updates quickly becomes increasingly important.

PatchWave is a set of specialized agents that uses static analysis tools on context we gather deterministically.

1. We pull the changelog, the code diff between versions, security advisories, and CI results.

2. The agent checks out your code in an isolated sandbox, where it uses structural code search, type checkers and your project's own toolchain to understand how your codebase uses each dependency being updated. Every Dependabot PR gets a report. You can see a few examples (against OSS repos) here: https://reports.patchwave.ai/alam00000/bentopdf/pull/913 and https://reports.patchwave.ai/shipshapecode/shepherd/pull/355...

3. If CI fails, we automatically dispatch a fix agent to try to get CI green again. For most PRs, this means updating your code to use a newer API, fixing linting/formatting issues, etc.

4. We have an optional feature that allows auto-merging certain PRs when PatchWave deems them as safe and the PR aligns with your auto-merge policy. Our recommended auto-merge policy is to auto-merge patch/minor/major dev dependencies and patch/minor production dependencies. You can customize this policy or turn auto-merge off entirely.

PatchWave will skip auto-merge in a bunch of cases where a human should review. For instance, if provenance changes (e.g., a package that's usually published by GitHub Actions via Trusted Publishing is suddenly published by an API Key), we require human review before merging. Dependabot also instituted an on-by-default 3-day cooldown to reduce the risk of supply chain attacks. If PatchWave makes any changes via a fix agent, we'll always require your review before merge.

Currently, PatchWave only works with Dependabot and GitHub. We plan to offer Renovate support in the future. We've eval'ed the agents the most against TypeScript and Ruby, but are always adding to our eval suite to improve accuracy. The fix agent works best with PRs that require modest code changes. For large updates, especially updates that span multiple majors, our fix agent will give up and provide you a remediation plan to help you mitigate.

On the privacy/security side of the house, our SOC 2 Type II audit is in progress (see trust.contextbridge.ai). We only run on repos you select, our agents run in a short-lived microVM per run, we use Amazon Bedrock with zero-data-retention, and never train on your code.

We're offering 25 free PRs per GitHub org, per month with no credit card required. Additional PRs are billed at about $1/PR, with discounts for higher volume. We also would love to accelerate OSS projects, so reach out to ask about additional free credits.

If you hate dealing with Dependabot PRs, we'd love for you to give it a shot and tell us what you think. Josh, Donnie, and I will be around answering any questions and responding to any feedback you have.

title: asktori
summary: Tori by TalkJS. AI support that's actually good

extra.author: skrebbel
extra.original_title: Show HN: Tori by TalkJS. AI support that's actually good

story_text.value:
Hey everyone!

Joshua and Egbert from TalkJS here. Today we're launching Tori, an AI support agent built for difficult product questions.

Other tools we tried struggled with the technical questions we get at TalkJS, so we built our own. One of our test questions was: "How can I add two-way sync between TalkJS and my Minecraft mod?"

Our docs never mention Minecraft, and TalkJS does not have a Java SDK. Tori figured out how a Java Edition mod could use Kotlin, found our Kotlin Data API even though it isn't mentioned on the homepage, and explained step-by-step how to connect the two. It avoided the obvious solution of REST + webhooks, and explained why that would be insecure in a clientside mod.

That's what it means for support to actually be good. Understand what customers are trying to build, research the features and limitations, and work out how they fit together. Tori works great even when no single page contains the answer.

Tori browses your live website and documentation, no retraining step. We've been using it for TalkJS support over the past few months, and it handles 87% of our customer enquiries autonomously.

Customers can ask for a human at any point, and you can always see what Tori is telling them and what it thinks. So your team can jump in and work alongside Tori, with the conversation and research already there. Our goal is for your customers to get good help faster, with human support always in reach.

Tori is built on TalkJS, whose infrastructure handles 130M+ monthly messages. The TalkJS base means you can fully customize the interface's components, layout and behavior to fit your product.

You also get direct access to senior Tori developers for free, including help with customization. We're launching early so customers can help shape the product.

Have a go at https://asktori.ai. We're curious what you think!

title: Alter (YC S25)
summary: Access control for multi-user agents

extra.author: simfinii
extra.original_title: Launch HN: Alter (YC S25) – Access control for multi-user agents

story_text.value:
Hi HN! We’re Srikar and Kevan, founders of Alter – https://alterauth.com/. We’re building access control for agents that can take actions on behalf of multiple users.

If you’ve built an internal agent people use through Slack, you may have experienced this scenario: everyone signs in with their own account, but the agent connects to the CRM or billing system with one shared API key, so the agent can do anything that the key can do. User-level authentication in Slack does nothing to control what the agent can do in an external system like the CRM or billing system.

Here’s what Alter does:

-It acts as a proxy and manages downstream credentials for every API request that an agent takes;

-It takes identity into account for every action the agent does. Automatically take into account the end user identity of the person that the agent is taking actions on behalf of.

-It enforces fine grained runtime policies and records compliance grade audit logs.

Here’s a demo video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=9ZqPU14ipGE

We started this because we saw first hand how hard it is to build agents in regulated industries. To unlock the true benefits of agents we need to allow agents to take actions, sometimes actions on behalf of end users. I (Srikar) was working at Goldmans and I saw how prohibitively expensive it was for me as a developer to write my own custom auth to enable multi-tenancy in agents and to allow agents to have strict policy controls as they act on behalf of end users. My co-founder, Kevan, is a second time founder and was previously working on a database startup. He has experience building and selling deep tech into highly regulated environments. So this problem seemed like a natural fit for the both of us.

Building and maintaining custom auth for multi tenant agents was challenging. But so was ensuring that the solution we developed was secure, scalable and keeping track of security grade audit logs. As a result we realized there needs to be a separate product category for this that enables developers to easily build secure multi user agents that can actually take actions in an enterprise. Some of the real-world use cases we’ve seen include:

We have built a multi user open claw for our own team using Alter that saved us countless hours on our GTM effort. Link here:https://github.com/AlterAIDev/openclaw-alter-plugin

We have multiple startups who have used our platform to build their own secure internal agents for everything ranging from SRE agents to back office agents dealing with Quickbooks and payroll platforms like Rippling. It has saved developers countless hours both in terms of building and maintenance. We also have a defense contractor building air gapped agents for marine corp using Alter.

Under the hood, the value that we provide is that we do a lot of the plumbing that no one wants to do. We support hundreds of providers, all manually tested end to end. Reliability is our biggest priority. We have built this in a way to allow developers to custom build their agents however they see fit. Everything ranging from custom policies, agent delegation, user attribution, audit logs needed for compliance to a LLM gateway with guardrails (Coming soon)

Building a security product is hard. We have learnt that in order to build a truly secure product, security thinking has to pervade every part of the development process. We have embraced shift left security. Every PR that is pushed out is continuously checked for supply chain attacks, potentially dangerous code patterns etc.

Our business plan revolved around usage based pricing. There is a free tier up to 10k requests and then a pricing tier starting beyond that. We would love it if people configured their APIs and OAuth credentials, tried out the policies and actually built agents that can take actions with alter!

If you’ve built an agent that acts for multiple users, how are you handling permissions today? We’d especially like to hear what you’ve had to build yourself.

https://alterauth.com/

title: Respan (YC W24)
summary: Open-source Rust AI gateway built around plugins

extra.author: Andydy25
extra.original_title: Launch HN: Respan (YC W24) – Open-source Rust AI gateway built around plugins

story_text.value:
Hey HN, this is Andy from Respan (https://www.respan.ai). We are building an open-source Rust AI gateway. It is a decoupled gateway, so everything is a plugin, including different providers, protocols (MCP, voice), modalities (images, videos), and gateway features (fallbacks, PII redaction, smart routing).

Instead of packaging tons of providers and features into one gateway, Respan provides a small core and public interfaces that teams can use to assemble the AI infrastructure their application needs. That way, users can build their own features as additional plugins without having to change the gateway's core.

Here’s a video demo: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=pVv2ibXiTXM

There are countless LLM gateways and most of them solve a common problem: calling different providers from a single endpoint. However, adding new features can become prohibitively difficult. So developers can end up building another gateway to solve a specific problem.

We've been building our gateway based on LiteLLM since 2024, and now it's providing services for thousands of orgs. Each org needs different API key settings, routes, and limits. To support that, we kept wrapping LiteLLM, adding more features to it, and at one stage, our wrapper code exceeded 100,000 lines.

This January, a routine LiteLLM upgrade caused intermittent connection errors, and we had to roll back. We still haven't figured out the cause, but since then, we no longer upgrade LiteLLM directly and instead manually backport upstream fixes. These experiences made us realize that continuing to patch LiteLLM is not a sustainable long-term solution, and we had to redesign the gateway ourselves.

While redesigning our gateway, we wanted to make it easier to add features without breaking existing ones. Inspired by Nginx, we think an AI gateway should have a really small core, only responsible for dispatching events.

We believe that everything should be a plugin in our gateway, including providers (OpenAI, Anthropic, Gemini), protocols (chat, realtime voice, MCP), modalities (images, videos), and gateway features for reliability and security (smart routing, fallbacks, and PII redaction through example plugins). Beyond that, we want developers to be able to easily extend the gateway's capabilities by adding their own plugins, without touching the core. Adding a provider, even your own, is dead simple, because quirks are plugins too and there’s nothing magical about them. A provider is a short file, Mistral’s is 22 lines, and each quirk, like Groq putting token usage in its own field, gets its own test.

Respan Gateway does more than let you call Claude or Gemini models from the OpenAI SDK. It handles tools, images, and reasoning protocols automatically: an application based on the OpenAI Realtime API can also use Gemini Live through the gateway, though not every feature translates. A simple chat app can use MCP tools configured in the gateway, without implementing MCP itself.

We also parse requests into a shared structure. When the client and provider use the same API, we preserve provider-specific fields in their native format, even if our shared structure doesn't have a field for them. That way, the gateway can write them back instead of dropping them.

Here’s how it works:

An adapter hands each HTTP or WebSocket connection to the first client format that recognizes it. The format exposes the request as a two-way stream of typed input and output events. The core runs plugins in registration order, allowing them to choose a provider, filter or wrap either stream, make additional calls, return a response, or refuse the request. A provider format then opens the upstream connection.

If the client and provider use the same format and no plugin changes the payload, the original bytes and protocol-specific fields can pass through unchanged. When formats differ, they translate through shared types for messages, tool calls, results, streams, and usage. This stream model can represent both one-shot HTTP requests and long-lived bidirectional sessions.

The gateway is open source at https://github.com/respanai/respan-gateway under the MIT or Apache-2.0 license. You don't need to use Respan's hosted platform and can run it directly on your local machine. Build it from source, add your provider keys, and swap the base URL in a supported client. You can keep using the API your client already speaks. It's still pre-alpha.

We make money from our hosted platform (https://www.respan.ai/pricing), which runs the gateway for you with native observability and evals, along with unified billing.

If you’re building routing, tools, filtering, observability, or security for agents, we'd love to see it as a plugin. PLUGINS.md in the repo explains how to write one and links to the plugins we’ve created so far. Turning that into an ecosystem is basically our roadmap, and we welcome you to contribute your own plugins. We'd love to answer any questions and hear your feedback!

https://github.com/respanai/respan-gateway

title: huggingface/transformers: Patch release v5.20.2
summary:
# Patch release: v5.20.2

This patch notably solves an issue where some inputs could loose their original type inside `prepare_inputs_for_generation` in `generate`, leading to problems with multimodal models. It also fixes some other issues listed on the below commits.

It contains the following commits:

- Fix inputs dict casting in generate (#49731) by @Cyrilvallez
- Fix zero expert gradients in bfloat16 with expert parallelism and ep_size < fsdp_size (#49688) by @qgallouedec 
- Declare the input modalities of the VLMs that report text only (#49677) by @qgallouedec 
- Avoid a host-to-device copy in eager_mask (#49684) by @hmellor
